guidance: A sizing aid, not a kernel rule: a watch on a directory covers that directory's entries only, so count every subdirectory, and remember that the watch and instance limits are per real user ID and shared with every other program the user runs.
method: inotify holds one watch per watched path: a directory watch reports events for entries in that directory, so a recursive watcher needs one watch per directory plus one per file it watches individually. Watches and instances are counted per real user ID, and fs.inotify.max_user_watches bounds the watch total, with inotify_add_watch failing with ENOSPC once it is reached; fs.inotify.max_user_instances bounds instance creation, and because a queue belongs to an instance every watching process needs one of its own. The planner multiplies directories plus individually watched files by the number of processes of one user, adds the entered headroom percentage, and rounds the watch target up to a whole watch. The queue target is the peak rate per instance times the longest drain interval, plus headroom, rounded up to a whole event; fs.inotify.max_queued_events caps an instance's queue at creation time and events beyond it are dropped with an IN_Q_OVERFLOW event delivered instead. The instances figure is shown as a floor because the limit is shared with other programs in the session. The sysctl snippet is built only when all three current limits are entered, and each value is the larger of the current and the target, so applying it can never lower a limit. Headroom, the drain interval and the peak rate are planning assumptions supplied by the user rather than kernel defaults. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
